newsitem.title: Australia: Australian man pleads innocent to mass murder.
newsitem.headline: Australian man pleads innocent to mass murder.

text.p: The man accused of the worst mass killing in modern Australian history pleaded not guilty to 35 counts of murder in a Tasmanian court on Monday.

Martin Bryant, 29, wore a faint smile as he denied a further 20 charges of attempted murder and 17 lesser charges arising from the massacre on April 28 at the historic penal colony of Port Arthur in the southern island state of Tasmania.
Bryant's not-guilty pleas means that the case will have to go to a full trial, expected to start on November 19 and run for three weeks. Bryant was remanded in custody until the trial.

The Supreme Court of Tasmania in the state capital of Hobart was ringed by heavy security for the hearing, the first time Bryant has appeared in person in court since his arrest the day after the killings.

In a 25-minute hearing, Bryant bent down to a microphone and answered "not guilty" in a soft, clear voice to all 72 charges as they were read in quick succession by the clerk of the court. No basis to his plea was either sought or offered.
Bryant stood beside a thick pane of shatter-proof glass separating him from the public gallery, and was flanked by three court security officers.
Dressed in a pale grey suit and with long, curly blond hair falling on to a white, collarless shirt, Bryant showed little emotion as he faced the judge.
He turned only once to face the courtroom where relatives of some of the dead sat in a packed public gallery only a few metres (yards) away.
"You are a bloody coward, Bryant," shouted Phillip Pears, after Bryant pleaded not guilty to murdering Pears' brother, Glenn -- the final charge of murder to be read out.
Ordered out of the court by the judge, Pears added before leaving: "Yours will come soon".

Bryant has been the subject of numerous death threats since his arrest outside the burning wreckage of the Seascape guest house near the sandstone ruins of the Port Arthur site. He left the court in a prison van escorted by eight police cars.
On April 28, a sunny Sunday afternoon, a lone gunman walked into the Broad Arrow Cafe at Port Arthur and shot 20 people as they ate their lunch.
Within an hour a further 12 people, including a three-year-old girl, were gunned down either outside the cafe, in their cars, or hiding behind a tree.
Three people were taken hostage and later found dead in the charred remains of the Seascape guest house.

Among the public gallery, crowded with Port Arthur residents and victims' family and friends, was Australian Linda White who carried her arm in a splint. She was shot near the guest house and is the subject of an attempted murder charge against Bryant.

The killings led Australia's conservative government to institute tough new gun laws under which high-powered and self-loading guns are banned. The law also established a national register of gun owners.

The law still has to be ratified by Australia's six states and two territories, which are responsible for gun laws. Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday he would talk with state leaders in the next few days to work out the details of a costly buy-back scheme for the outlawed weapons.
